messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marianne is a 61-year-old policy analyst who came to treatment more than a year after a toxic chemical exposure in her office building. She had been at work late, reviewing regulatory language with two colleagues, when a sharp burnt odor began moving through the ventilation system. At first she assumed it was an electrical problem, but within minutes the smell thickened into something acrid and chemical, mixed with a faint alcohol-like note from industrial solvents. People in the hallway started coughing. Marianne remembers the confusion most vividly: no one seemed to know whether to evacuate, which stairwell was safe, or how serious the leak was. She froze long enough to feel she had already made the wrong choice. By the time she got outside, her heart was pounding, her chest was tight, and she was overcome by the conviction that she had failed at the one thing that should have been simple—getting herself to safety.

Since then, smells have become the quickest way back into that moment. The odor of smoke from a neighbor’s fireplace, a burnt smell from toast in the office break room, even the alcohol smell of cleaning products in conference rooms can make her body jolt before she has fully identified what she is smelling. In those moments Marianne does not simply feel reminded; she immediately questions herself. She has come to believe that if she could miss danger once, she cannot rely on herself to judge a situation correctly, and the sudden rush in her body feels like proof. What unsettles her most is how quickly these reactions turn into the thought that something in her has changed permanently, that she will never feel normal emotions again and will only ever have alarm.

That loss of confidence has shaped the way she moves through her days. Because she no longer trusts herself to do the right thing instinctively, Marianne tries to think her way into safety. She repeatedly goes over the exposure in her mind, replaying where she was sitting, whether she should have recognized the odor sooner, whether she should have told others to leave immediately. She tells herself that if she can finally work out how it could have been prevented, she might not make the same mistake again. She also avoids television dramas, news coverage, or articles about fires, leaks, or industrial accidents, not because she finds them merely unpleasant but because she fears that being pulled back into those memories will confirm how emotionally damaged she has become. Yet the more time she spends ruminating and narrowing what she can tolerate, the more inadequate she feels. Instead of restoring confidence, these habits leave her more doubtful, more convinced she cannot depend on her own judgment.

Her work as a policy analyst keeps her in exactly the kinds of environments that now feel dangerous to her. Entering a meeting room, Marianne first looks for exits and only then for colleagues. She chooses seats near the door, or against a wall where she feels less exposed, and quietly tracks ventilation grates, electrical smells, and who seems to notice them. She scans buildings automatically now, a habit that feels necessary because she no longer believes she would respond effectively without constant vigilance. At the same time, living in that state of readiness has deepened the same beliefs. When her heart lurches during an ordinary staff meeting because someone reheated food and left a burnt smell in the corridor, she reads her need to locate the nearest exit as evidence that she is no longer a person who can simply walk into a room and be fine. The threat feels ever-present, and her dependence on these precautions becomes, in her mind, further proof of weakness.

This has narrowed her life in ways her husband has noticed. She still goes to work, but she arrives early so she can choose where to sit in conference rooms before others come in. She has started declining off-site meetings in older buildings and will leave windows open at home if a burnt odor from outside drifts in, even in cold weather. On one recent evening, the smell of rubbing alcohol in a medical office waiting room combined with a faint scorched smell from nearby construction, and she became so physically reactive—sweating, trembling, unable to focus on the receptionist’s words—that she had to step outside. What frightened her afterward was not only the intensity of the reaction, but the way it sharpened her conviction that she cannot trust herself and that the world is full of cues she may miss until it is too late. Because she now enters places already scanning for danger, she notices smells immediately; because she notices them so quickly, they strike with even more force.

Marianne finally sought help after realizing that her life was being organized around escape routes, smell checks, and private mental reviews of what she should have done differently. She says she wants “to feel like a person again,” but what she fears most is that this constant alertness means the exposure revealed something fundamentally unreliable in her, and that one day she will again face danger and fail herself.
